I'm writing a data-driven story for ConsumerAffairs ranking the 100 largest U.S. metros by how much property taxes have risen relative to home values in the last few years. Looking for these qualified US-based experts who can provide insightful written responses to a few questions (more detailed answers to a couple will be more helpful than surface-level ones to all): - Property tax/public finance experts - Housing economists/real estate economists - Urban economics/local government finance academics - Property tax policy researchers - Assessors or assessment professionals 1. Why do property taxes rise? Can you explain how property taxes work and why they can vary so much from one place to another? 2. What can homeowners do about rising property taxes? Please share 3-5 actionable tips and briefly explain each. 3. Sometimes a metro's home values fall slightly, and property taxes fall even more sharply the same year. What usually explains taxes moving faster than values in a case like that? 4. Property tax growth can look very different for homeowners with a mortgage vs. one without in the same metro. What usually drives that gap? 5. It's rare, but occasionally a metro sees property tax bills fall over a two-year period even as home values rise. What would typically cause that? 6. A metro can have one of the highest dollar property tax bills in the country while its effective tax rate (tax as a % of home value) is flat or falling. How should homeowners think about that difference? 7. When people look at their tax bill, is nominal dollar growth misleading compared to what's happened after inflation? How big a difference does that usually make? Finally, please provide: 1) source's role/title, LinkedIn profile, company website, and company descriptor 2) source's email IMPORTANT: NO AI responses, or responses you've already submitted elsewhere. Given the volume of source requests I send out, I can't respond to check-ins. Rest assured that if your response is a strong fit, I'll use it. I also don't have visibility into publish dates once a piece is with editorial, so I can't provide those either. Thanks so much for understanding! _____

This source request is for an interview that will become an article in the Reputation Intelligence newsletter on the Substack platform and shared on the LinkedIn platform in a post. If this appeals to you, please closely read the brief, important points below before proceeding to the interview questions and precisely following the instructions. --------------------------------------- 1. Briefly introduce yourself. 2. Please, no use of AI. I value your brain, not answers from technology. Please don't use AI in any form in your reply. 3. Copy and paste the questions (and question numbers) into your reply. Create a new paragraph, with a double space between the question and your answer. This is easier on my eyes and brain. 4. No backlinks offered yet your name, brief professional title, expertise and business are highlighted and added to article tags for SEO and AI finding purposes. 5. Please send a professional headshot, perfectly focused and medium large to accompany the article, to rep.intel.news@gmail.com ------------------------ INTERVIEW Copy and paste the questions (and question numbers into your reply and double space between each question and your answers). No AI in your responses. 1) Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei: "I won't lie to you—there are real dangers," Amodei told CBS. "And I think for too long the industry lied to people about the fact that this technology had risks." This can't be a throwaway line and seems like it should be discussed. Whether it was ignorance of as Amodei said, a lie, how does this affect the trust levels and benefit of the doubt between AI leaders and their companies with government, the media, investors and the general public? Are they worthy of forgiveness or amplified scrutiny? 2) "I don't think I fully just appreciated what it would actually be like when the progress was as fast as it was," he added, which seems to be a little more believable. How much should government, media and the public take that point into consideration when judging AI leaders and their judgment? 3) "It doesn't mean we need to panic today,” Amodei told CBS. “It doesn't mean we need to shut it all down. But I would say it's a warning sign. It's a warning sign that we need to slow down." Why was pace not a concern until now or at least as much of one as it should have been all along? What has been getting in the way and what errors were glaring? _____
